text.en: Meena saw a road sign near her school. "Why must we obey signs?" she asked.

Road safety means following rules to prevent accidents. Many accidents are caused by overspeeding, drunk driving, not wearing helmets or seat belts and breaking signals.
Road signs are of three kinds: mandatory (orders, such as stop), cautionary (warnings, such as a school ahead) and informatory (information such as a hospital). Traffic lights have red for stop, yellow for get ready and green for go.
Pedestrians should use footpaths and zebra crossings, drivers must wear helmets or seat belts and keep to the speed limit. Learning first aid helps in an emergency, and the Motor Vehicles Act sets penalties.
Road safety means following rules to prevent accidents.

text.en: Road crashes are one of the leading preventable causes of injury among young people in India. Understanding road rules saves lives every single day.

board.text: Road crashes are preventable

text.en: Most road accidents happen because of human error: overspeeding, drunk driving, jumping red lights, talking on mobile phones while driving, and failing to wear helmets or seatbelts.

board.text: Main causes: speed, phones, alcohol, no helmet

text.en: Other contributing factors include poorly lit roads, potholes, overloaded vehicles, worn tyres, brake failure and sudden animal crossings.

board.text: Road & vehicle factors matter too

text.en: Let us learn the three families of road signs by their shape so you recognise them in a split second. Mandatory or Regulatory signs are circles—usually with a red border—telling you what you must or must not do.

board.text: Circles = Mandatory signs (Stop, No Entry)

text.en: Cautionary or Warning signs are red-bordered triangles warning you of hazards ahead, such as a sharp bend, narrow bridge, school zone or railway crossing.

board.text: Triangles = Warning signs (School, Bend)

text.en: Informatory signs are blue or green rectangles showing helpful services like hospitals, petrol pumps, parking areas, bus stops and highway distances.

board.text: Rectangles = Information signs (Hospital, P)

text.en: Traffic signals speak a universal colour code: red means complete stop behind the stop line, amber means prepare to stop and clear the junction safely, and green means proceed only when the way is clear.

board.text: Red = Stop, Amber = Caution, Green = Go

text.en: Pedestrians have vital safety habits too: always walk on the footpath, or if there is none, walk facing oncoming traffic so you can see approaching vehicles.

board.text: No footpath -> walk facing oncoming traffic

text.en: Cross only at zebra crossings, pedestrian subways or foot overbridges. Before stepping off the kerb, always look right, then left, then right again.

board.text: Cross at zebra lines: look right, left, right

text.en: Never run across a road from behind a parked bus or car, because approaching drivers cannot see you until it is too late.

board.text: Never dart out behind parked vehicles

text.en: For cyclists and two-wheeler riders, an ISI-marked helmet strapped firmly reduces the risk of fatal head injury by over seventy percent.

board.text: ISI helmet cuts fatal head injury risk

text.en: Under the Motor Vehicles Act, riding a motorised two-wheeler without a valid licence, triple riding, and underage driving are illegal and dangerous.

board.text: No underage driving or triple riding

text.en: Inside cars and buses, front and rear seatbelts stop passengers from being thrown forward during sudden braking. Children should sit safely in the back seat.

board.text: Seatbelts protect every passenger

text.en: Remember the 'Golden Hour'—the first sixty minutes after a serious road crash. Rapid first aid and hospital care during this hour dramatically increase survival.

board.text: Golden Hour: first 60 minutes save lives

text.en: India's Good Samaritan Law protects kind bystanders who help accident victims reach a hospital from police harassment or unnecessary legal trouble.

board.text: Good Samaritan Law protects helpers

text.en: Know the emergency numbers by heart: dial 108 for free emergency ambulance service and 112 for the national all-in-one emergency helpline.

board.text: Emergency numbers: 108 (Ambulance), 112 (SOS)

text.en: Educators summarise road safety through the four Es: Engineering better roads, Enforcement of traffic laws, Education of citizens, and Emergency medical care.

board.text: 4 Es: Engineering, Enforcement, Education, Emergency

text.en: Never use headphones or stare at a phone screen while crossing a street or cycling—your ears and eyes are your earliest warning sensors.

board.text: Stay alert: no phones/earphones on roads

text.en: At night or in heavy rain, wear light-coloured or reflective clothing and keep bicycle reflectors and lights working so drivers spot you from afar.

board.text: Visibility saves lives at night & in rain

text.en: In school zones, speed limits drop sharply and students should board or alight from school buses only after the bus comes to a complete halt.

board.text: Wait for full stop before boarding buses

text.en: Keep a safe stopping distance from the vehicle ahead—at higher speeds, braking distance grows much faster than speed itself.

board.text: Higher speed = much longer stopping distance

text.en: Always give way to ambulances and fire engines with flashing sirens; seconds saved can save a stranger's life.

board.text: Always yield to ambulances & fire engines

text.en: To judge any road situation safely, apply the three-second rule: spot the sign shape, check blind spots, and choose patience over haste.

board.text: Patience beats haste on every road

text.en: Road safety is a shared civic duty—when every pedestrian, cyclist and driver obeys the rules, everyone reaches home safely.

board.text: Obey rules -> everyone gets home safely

problem.en: While cycling to school, you see a red-bordered triangular sign showing two children walking, and a school bus stops ahead. What do the sign and situation require you to do?

text.en: Decode the road sign by its shape.

why.en: A red-bordered triangle is a Cautionary (Warning) sign—here warning of a School Zone ahead.

text.en: Anticipate hidden hazards near the stopped bus.

why.en: Students may step out suddenly in front of or behind the bus.

text.en: Take the safe action.

why.en: Slow down early, ring your bell gently if needed, keep wide clearance, and stop if children are crossing.
